https://www.dw.com/en/spain-thieves-stea.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JXKN The Bronze age collection's historical value is incalculable, but even the gold is worth a pretty penny if melted down and therefore lost forever [FILE: Nov 10, 2016] Image: Lanmas/Visually/picture alliance Advertisement Thieves on Thursday raided one of the world's greatest Bronze Age gold collections in the latest of a series of high-profile heists on European museums in recent months. The early morning raid on Villena Museum in eastern Spain lasted just a few minutes. A group of thieves described by one official as "super-fast and super-professional" made off with almost the entire Treasure of Villena collection, leaving behind only a few items. What happened in the heist? "The alarm at the Villena Museum went off around 5:20 a.m.," said a spokesman for the town council, adding that within four minutes, they had all left the building again in an extremely rapid and professional operation. The collection of Bronze Age gold, some of which we now know hailed from a meteorite, was a centerpiece at the small museum in the Alicante province. "They've taken most of the treasure," the mayor of Villena, Fulgencio Cerdan told journalists. "We are absolutely devastated, I'm even trembling. The truth is that for those of us from Villena, this destroys us. It's part of our heritage, our wealth." The thieves arrived in several vehicles and apparently entered the museum "through a window," according to the Spanish government's deputy representative in Alicante, Manuel Pineda. Mayor Cerdan said that only three silver vessels, a bracelet, an earring and one of four crowns in the collection — which the thieves appeared to have "dropped" while making their exit — remained behind. "All security systems were activated," according to the Villena spokesman, who insisted there had been "no failure" by the museum. The collection was discovered more than 60 years ago and is thought to be a little more than 3,000 years old Image: Museo de Villena What is the Treasure of Villena? The Treasure of Villena is a collection of more than 50 mainly gold objects, discovered in 1963 by archaeologist Jose Maria Soler in a sunken vessel in a dried out riverbed. They are dated to between 1300 and 1000 BCE. The gold pieces include 11 bowls, three bottles and 28 bracelets. The collection has been exhibited beyond Villena in cities including Madrid, Alicante, Tokyo and Kyoto, and two sets of replicas were later made to showcase the collection without taking it away from the armored display at the Villena Archaeological Museum. The relics' historical value is incalculable, although thieves might struggle to sell them even on the black market after having famously lifted them from a well-known display. The mayor said the gold alone would be worth around €1.7 million or $2 million. According to the museum's website, specialist researchers consider it the most important collection of gold tableware from the Bronze Age. It also represents the earliest known example of iron use in Western Europe, two pieces crafted from a metal that recent studies showed hailed from a meteor. The collection includes some of the oldest known iron metalwork, seemingly thanks to the raw materials landing as part of a meteorite Image: Museo de Villena Several slick heists on European museums recently, most famously the Louvre Thursday's lightning dawn raid is the latest in a series on European museums in the last year. Most famously, the Louvre Museum was hit in broad daylight last October , escaping in less than 10 minutes with jewelry worth millions. This led to the director's eventual resignation and a protracted political scandal, as well as forcing part of the museum to close for an extended period . Italy's Culture Ministry announced on Sunday that four works of "extraordinary value" by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Sicily . Shortly before that, Italian police said they had recovered three paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse stolen from a museum near Parma . Again this involved a highly-organized group of thieves who were in and out in a matter of minutes. https://www.dw.com/en/saudi-arabia-secon.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O802 Riyadh airport will be closed until at least Sunday night [FILE: 2019] Image: Valery Sharifulin/TASS/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement At least one person was killed and 11 others were injured in a stike on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Sunday, a day after a similar attack killed 12 and injured hundreds . "King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was subjected to a new attack on Sunday afternoon," the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement. It later confirmed that the individual killed in the Sunday attack was a Pakistani national. A spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said that a cruise missile had been intercepted by air defense systems in the vicinity of the airport, but no further details were immediately available. The Houthis later claimed responsibility for the strikes, saying they had "carried out four qualitative operations in the past 24 hours using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones." A spokesman said the group targeted the Riyadh airport multiple times, as well as the Dammam airport in the east of the country and two facilities belonging to the Saudi state oil company Aramco. Later on Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed an attack on Dammam airport. Houthis warn airlines after deadly Riyadh airport strike To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Houthis warn airlines to avoid Saudi Arabia The latest Houthi strikes also came just hours after the rebel group warned airlines and travelers to avoid Saudi airports. "We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our forces," read a statement released by the group on social media. It added that airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina would not be targeted. "We ‌urge everyone to take our warnings seriously," the statement continued, stating: "Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions." What now for Saudi Arabia after Riyadh airport attack? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Why are Saudi airports being targeted? Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the rebels seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, including around the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Houthi-run health authority claimed this weekend that 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in the last five weeks, 60% of them women and children. Earlier on Sunday, it said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa. The Houthi-run Al Masirah TV also reported that Saudi Arabia had struck the international airport in Sanaa on Sunday afternoon. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims. "Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," the Houthi-run Foreign Ministry said in statements carried by Al Masirah TV on Sunday, adding that its ​actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity. What has Saudi Arabia said about the Riyadh airport attacks? The Saudi-led coalition, which supports the internationally recognized Yemeni government in its conflict against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, vowed a tough response to the attack, which it labeled a "full-fledged war crime." The Houthi strikes on Riyadh come amid a surge in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia this week, which have targeted other airports, military sites and oil infrastructure. The spike in attacks has followed a major military offensive by the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis. The rebels, one of Tehran's regional proxies , have been fighting Yemen's government, which is recognized by the international community, since the outbreak of a civil war over a decade ago. While a truce in 2022 froze the conflict, it failed to secure a lasting peace deal. The US-Israeli war with Iran has seen fighting flare up again in Yemen, worsening an already severe humanitarian crisis . Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video How has the international community reacted to the Riyadh strikes? US President Donald Trump on Saturday said he would be speaking to Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in the wake of the attack, which he said was "not acceptable." Trump also said that the US was "going to look" at potentially joining Saudi strikes against the rebels. On Sunday, European leaders expressed their "shock" at the attack on Riyadh airport. The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU stands in "solidarity with Saudi Arabia" as she condemned the "dangerous escalation." "These attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shock waves sent through the world," von der Leyen said. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul "firmly" condemned what he described as "a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation". "Our thoughts are with the victims and I send my sincere condolences to their loved ones," he said on X. UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting slammed the attacks as "contemptible" and a "dangerous escalation," while the French Foreign Ministry condemned the "heinous attack" and stressed its "total solidarity" with Saudi Arabia. Russia, which is a strategic partner of Iran, also condemned the Houthis' attack and called for the hostilities to end "through political and diplomatic means." Australia, meanwhile, has urged its citizens in the Saudi capital to "shelter in place" amid the escalating attacks. Why can't the Saudis defeat the Houthis?
